query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled pre-oxidation treatment that selectively promotes the formation of a Cr-rich oxide tribofilm on the FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating will enhance its high-temperature wear resistance by creating a self-healing, load-bearing and lubricious surface layer.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin protective coating with a fine-grained microstructure and no engineered oxide layer on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled pre-oxidation treatment (optimizing temperature, time, and oxygen partial pressure) designed to selectively oxidize the surface and enrich it in Cr, relative to the untreated as-deposited coating.
generation.conditions: High-load sliding wear tests conducted at elevated temperatures in the range of approximately 500°C to 700°C.
generation.structural_mediator: A coherent, self-healing, Cr-rich oxide tribofilm that forms on the coating surface during pre-oxidation and remains adherent during wear.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures under sliding conditions, the pre-oxidized surface facilitates the formation of a protective and continuously regenerating Cr-rich oxide layer. This tribofilm acts as a barrier against direct metal-to-metal contact, lowering friction and wear by bearing the sliding load and providing lubricious behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline as-deposited coating, the pre-oxidized coating will exhibit a lower wear rate and a more stable/lower coefficient of friction under high-temperature, high-load sliding conditions, attributable to the presence of a coherent, self-healing oxide layer.
generation.baseline: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating without any engineered or pre-formed oxide layer.
generation.boundary: Tested under high-load sliding wear at temperatures between 500°C and 700°C; the hypothesis applies only if the selective oxidation yields a continuous, adherent, and self-healing Cr-rich oxide tribofilm.
generation.uncertainty: The exact phase composition, thickness, and long-term durability of the formed oxide layer under cyclic thermal and mechanical loads remain uncertain and require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coated samples on conventional metal substrates: (1) a baseline as-deposited group and (2) a group undergoing controlled pre-oxidation treatment to induce selective Cr oxidation. Subject both groups to high-load sliding wear tests at 500°C–700°C, while monitoring friction and wear rates over multiple cycles.
measurements: Wear rate (mass loss or depth of wear scar)
Surface composition and oxide layer coherence (using XPS, SEM, and TEM)
Continuity and self-healing behavior of the oxide tribofilm (via repeated cycling and microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and improved friction stability compared to the baseline, or if no coherent, Cr-rich oxide tribofilm is observed during or after wear testing, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In this paper, the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating was prepared on MoNbTaTiW RHEA by a fused slurry method. The microstructural evolution and compositions of the silicide coating under high-temperature oxidation environment were studied. The results show that the silicide coating could effectively prevent the oxidation of the MoNbTaTiW RHEA. The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure: a high silicon content layer mainly composed of MSi 2 as the outer layer and a low silicon content layer mainly contained M 5 Si 3 as the inner layer. Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the silicon element diffused from the silicide coating to the RHEA substrate while the oxidation of the coating occurred. After oxidation, the coating was composed of an outer oxide layer and an inner silicide layer. The silicide layer moved toward the inside of the substrate, led to the increase of its thickness. Compared with the initial silicified layer, its structure did not change significantly. The structure and compositions of the oxide layer on the outer surface strongly depended on the oxidation temperature. Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. The CrMoNbWV HEA has comparable mechanical and corrosive properties with the WNbMoTaV type HEA, but at the same time has a reduced density: CrMoNbWV—10.55 g/cm

frame.system: FeNiCrCoCu used as a thin-film protective coating on a conventional metal substrate. The starting state is an as-deposited microstructure with a fine grain structure and no engineered oxide layer.
frame.goal: Explain and improve the overall high‐temperature wear resistance of the coating by identifying the mechanistic role of thermally activated surface transformations.
frame.limitation: Previous studies mainly focused on room‐temperature wear and addressed the alloy’s composition, grain size, and substrate interactions over a limited thermal regime, not capturing the full wear response of the coating at elevated temperatures.
constraints: FeNiCrCoCu must remain a thin protective coating
Expense favors its use as a coating on conventional metals rather than in bulk
High-temperature wear is the target application
Intervention must be relative to a baseline as-deposited coating condition
frame.regime: Elevated temperatures (e.g., approximately 500°C to 700°C) under high contact load and sliding wear conditions.
prior_attempts: Studies have examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to alloy composition, grain size, and coating–substrate pairs
These approaches fell short by not addressing the integrated behavior of the coating across a broader high-temperature range or focusing on dynamic surface evolution during wear.
frame.understanding: Hypothesis: At high temperatures, the FeNiCrCoCu coating undergoes selective oxidation that leads to the formation of a self-healing, adherent oxide tribofilm (enriched in elements such as Cr) which plays a key role in reducing wear by serving as a lubricious, load-bearing barrier during sliding. Intervention: Modify the surface via a controlled pre-oxidation treatment relative to the untreated (baseline) as-deposited coating. If the hypothesis is correct, the pre-oxidized coating will exhibit a lower wear rate and more stable friction behavior under high-temperature (500°C–700°C) and high-load sliding conditions compared to the baseline. Prior evidence linking selective oxidation in similar alloys to improved wear performance supports this mechanism. Conversely, if controlled oxidation does not lead to the formation of a coherent, protective tribofilm or if wear resistance does not improve relative to the baseline, then that outcome would falsify the hypothesis.

decision.trend: Initial studies on HEA wear behavior focused on room‐temperature tests, examining the influence of alloy composition, grain size, and coating–substrate interactions. Later work shifted towards high‐temperature regimes, where researchers observed that dynamic surface transformations—particularly the formation of oxide phases (such as spinels)—could improve wear resistance. However, even these studies did not integrate an approach that proactively induces and tests a self‐healing oxide tribofilm under high-load, high-temperature wear conditions.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear whether a deliberately engineered, selective oxidation can generate a coherent, self-healing oxide tribofilm (with envisioned Cr enrichment) that significantly improves high-temperature wear resistance of the FeNiCrCoCu coating compared to the baseline as-deposited state.
decision.lever: Implement a controlled pre-oxidation treatment designed to selectively oxidize the surface (optimizing temperature, duration, and ambient oxygen partial pressure to promote Cr-rich oxide formation) and then compare the wear performance against the as-deposited coating.
decision.why: This intervention follows the trend that high-temperature activation leads to beneficial oxide formation in similar HEA coatings. By deliberately inducing a selective, self-healing oxide layer, the experiment directly tests the mechanistic hypothesis that such a tribofilm serves as a lubricious, load-bearing barrier, improving wear resistance at 500–700°C under high-load sliding conditions. An absence of improved wear behavior or failure to detect a coherent tribofilm would falsify the hypothesis.
